ALL NOTES

NIGHT // ROLL

The chiptune DAW that teaches you composition — a piano roll and an engraved score over one timeline, authentic 2A03 chip audio, and an annotation layer that lives with the notes. This site is where it was built: by studying the Final Fantasy I soundtrack, captured note-for-note from the actual NES sound chip.

House rule: keys, meters, and chords are the analyst's discoveries. The app displays evidence and records verdicts — it never decides them for you.

Sounds: FluidR3_GM by Frank Wen (MIT), via Benjamin Gleitzman's midi-js-soundfonts (MIT). Notation: VexFlow (MIT). Night Roll itself: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 — free for personal and noncommercial use; selling or republishing it is not permitted.

Josh Cough & Claude, 2026 · github.com/Night-Roll-App/night-roll

Status

DRUM PATTERN

from bar beat to bar beat grid

One bar of pattern, repeated across the bar range on the drums track (created if the song has none). Tap cells to toggle.

TRANSPOSE

Chromatic moves everything blindly by semitones. In key moves each note to the next scale degree of the declared key — a "whole step up that stays in the key," so some notes move 1 and some move 2. One ⟲ per tap.

INSERT TIME

Opens a gap: everything from the insert point onward slides right; a section or chord that starts before and is still open at the point stretches instead; one that ends exactly at the point stays put. Notes, sections, chords, the loop — all carried. One ⟲ undoes it.

At  bar beat
Insert

GRID

How many lines per bar. Tap a number — the roll redraws instantly and pencil, drags and resizes snap to those lines. The song itself never changes.

Anchor:  bar beat

DIVIDE INTO

Each selected note becomes N equal notes — pitch, velocity, and total length unchanged. 3 on a half note = quarter-note triplets; 3 on a quarter = eighth triplets; 6 on two beats = a run of six. One ⟲ undoes it.

QUANTIZE

Snaps each selected note's start to the current grid (the same grid Move and Pencil use — 16ths, triplet steps with a T duration active, or 32nds once the song has any). 100% lands exactly on the line; 75%/50% is a softer nudge, partway there — good for a raw take that's close but not glued to the grid. One ⟲ undoes the whole selection.

NIGHT ROLL — WHAT YOU CAN DO

🎓 Learning mode
Tap it in View ▾ → 🎓 Learning mode (or Settings → Other) to switch off. On (the default on a device that's been used for analysis before): meter, key and chord names stay undeclared until you work them out yourself — a lasso still lists the notes, Chord? stays hidden so you name it first, and the LCD reads the usual "4/4?" / "C?" until you've earned the real answer. Off (Normal): lasso'd chords name themselves, an unset meter/key shows a labelled estimate (LCD "Gm~", the key picker's "estimated — tap to set") instead of the plain default — estimates are never written as a real annotation until you tap "Set this key". A little 🎓 in the LCD marks Learning; the toggle is one device-global switch, not per song.
⇄ Compare with repo
View → Compare with repo (or the Compare button on a song's "music edited" line in the Publish sheet) fetches the song's published copy and outlines every difference on the roll: gold = a note only in your version, red = a note only in the published copy, both on a note whose length or velocity changed; dashed outlines mark notes that are not in the version you are hearing. The bar above the roll counts them and its button swaps which version plays — hear the published copy swaps its notes in (the song is read-only until you swap back; nothing is written, your draft stays yours), hear your version swaps them back. ✕ on the bar leaves compare. Works on your own songs that have been published; turn a chop off first.
▾ Hide controls
The ▾ at the footer's left folds the bottom controls (edit row + footer) away so small screens show music instead of buttons — a floating ▴ brings them back. Phones start folded automatically; your explicit choice is remembered per device.
Closing a sheet
Every sheet closes three ways: tap the dimmed area outside it, tap the ✕ pinned to its top-right (it stays put while a long sheet scrolls, so the notes list never makes you scroll to the bottom to get out), or press Esc. Esc closes the topmost one, so stacked sheets unstack one at a time. Saving or sending closes the sheet for you. The only exception is a confirm box — it asked a question, so it waits for an answer.
𝄞 Score / ▦ Roll
Switch between piano roll and engraved sheet music. Same timeline, same everything else. Your choice is remembered.
Drag / pinch
One finger pans; two fingers zoom — spread horizontally to stretch time, vertically to grow/shrink the pitch rows (roll only). Two fingers moving TOGETHER pan — and that works with pencil or select armed; anything the first finger started is rolled back the instant the second finger lands. With an Apple Pencil (or one finger), hold to grab: dwell about a quarter second on a note before it drags, and the pencil tool only places a note on a clean tap or a dwell — a fast passing stroke always PANS, so sweeping across the song never moves a note or plants a stray one. A mouse grabs instantly (pressing a mouse button is already deliberate); the Apple Pencil can too — Settings → Other → "Apple Pencil draws and grabs at once" (off by default: with it on, a Pencil swipe that starts on a note moves the note instead of scrolling). Songs open fitted to the screen. In score view, scroll fully left to see the clefs and key signature.
Roll zoom-out limit
Pinch-out stops once the whole song is in view — per axis: when every bar fits, further pinch-out only reveals pitch; when every note is visible — plus a few rows of breathing room above and below, so the top notes never sit against the ruler — it stops. Opening a song lands exactly on this limit.
Score zoom limit
The score stops zooming out where its busiest bar would overflow — engraved notes can't shrink. Mute dense tracks to zoom out further, or use the Roll for the bird's-eye view.
▶ Play / ■ Stop
NES-style voices; drum tracks get a real kit. Songs loop at their final bar forever (album play, below, is what ends them). While a song is still loading its sound — the console's voice, game or SoundFont instruments, a recording — ▶ shows ⏳ 42% and waits; tap it then and it plays by itself the moment the sound is ready (tap again to cancel); a load that fails lets you play anyway and says why.
Playing in the background
In the installed iPad app, music keeps playing when you leave the app or lock the screen: start a song or an album, then switch away. Come back to see where it is.
💿 Play album
In File → Open…, every album has a 💿 Play album row at the top (it starts from the song you have open when that song is in the album). The album plays straight through like a record — each song gets its intro plus two passes of its loop, fades, and the next one loads (the console's own sound is waited for while it renders) — and wraps around to the first song forever. While it plays, a 💿 strip under the transport shows 3/19, the song, and what's next, with ⏮ Prev, ⏭ Next, and ✕ to leave. ▶, ■, ⏮ and Space work on the current song exactly as always (■ just pauses the album; ▶ picks it back up). Picking another song, ●, or Download audio also leaves. No dialog will interrupt a run: a song with a newer save on the repo plays from this device's draft and says so. Editing while it plays is fine. Keep the screen on — locking the iPad pauses it, and unlocking picks up where it stopped. While a run is on, the address bar carries it too (?album=) — opening that link reopens with the strip up, run armed, same song selected, and nothing playing yet; the first ▶ plays it as an album pass, same as picking 💿 Play album.
⏱ Metronome
Tap ⏱ to turn the click on or off; ⚙ beside it opens the settings. Any meter (1–12 over 2/4/8/16 — bpm counts the denominator beat), tap each beat cell to cycle accent → normal → silent, subdivisions in 2/3/4, slider or tap-tempo. Three modes: free-running (its own clock); follow song — clicks ride the song's own grid, phase-perfect on the declared meter through tempo changes, speed slider, and loops; trial meter — click a meter of YOUR choosing over the real music to A/B candidates by ear (the "shift accents" ‹ › slides the pattern's starting beat, since a right meter can sit offset). Settings stick.
Count-in
Optional one-bar click lead-in. Playing counts in only from bar 1 beat 1 — never mid-song, never when the song loops back around; recording (●) counts in from wherever it starts, so a punch-in at bar 17 gets its bar of clicks too.
⏮
Back to bar 1.
Speed slider
25–200% of the song's own tempo, for close listening or instrument practice — pitch stays true; only time stretches. Applies when you let go; keeps its setting across songs. A 100% button appears whenever you're off native — tap to snap back.
Scroll while playing
Scrolling away suspends the auto-follow camera so you can study any spot; it latches back on when the playhead reaches what you're looking at.
▤ Tracks view
The arrangement view (𝄞/▤/▦ button cycles Roll → Tracks → Score; also in View ▾): one lane per track, its notes drawn as a thumbnail (each lane scaled to its own range), with the track's color dot, name, M/S, and a volume fader in the lane header — the fader saves as the same vol= annotation as the voice menu's. Tap a note to select it (it sounds); lasso a box and it selects by TIME across every lane it touches — cross-track selection in one gesture. Hold-to-grab a selected note and drag: sideways moves it in time (bar-magnet-free, 16th snap), and dragging up or down carries the whole selection to another lane — pitch kept, one ⟲ undoes it, drums and melodic lanes never mix. Dragging shows a ghost until you release. Tap a lane's header to select that track; tap the selected track's header again for its voice & volume menu. Pencil doesn't draw here (a squeezed lane has no honest pitch) — it draws in Roll or Score; Erase works. The ruler above is the same one as always: sections, cycle, magnetic bars, the playhead triangle.
🎸 Bassist
The 🎸 beside 🎲 (behind ⋯, or Edit ▾ → Bassist…) generates a bassline for the range onto a track you pick (defaults to a NEW bass track unless an empty one exists — it never silently overwrites your notes; the status line says exactly what it replaces). PITCHES COME FROM YOUR DECLARED CHORDS — chord tones, slash basses honored (C♯/F walks to the F), N.C. bars pedal the key root; gaps ride the last chord. With ONLY a melody and no chords, it sketches the melody's harmony internally (duration-weighted, strong beats count more) and plays bass under that sketch — the sketch is never shown or written anywhere, and different seeds read the melody differently, which is the idea machine — declared chords always win bar-by-bar, inference only fills the unannotated gaps. The bass PLAYS THROUGH your Break sections (a Break is bass-alone by your own device). Styles: chug (root 8ths), pump (root–fifth), arp (chord tones cycling), walk (approach notes INTO each coming chord — the leading-tone move, mechanized), riff (rhythm copied from the follow source: the kick, any track, or the chord changes). busy 1–5, octave 1–3, strictly monophonic (NES-legal), same take chips / one-⟲ replace / same-label-sections-restate contract as the Drummer.
⊞ Insert bars
Edit ▾ → Insert bars… opens a gap anywhere in the song: pick the spot (bar + beat, decimals fine), how much (a count of bars, beats, or 16ths), and Insert. Everything from that point onward — notes, sections, chords, keys, the loop point — slides right together. A section that starts before the point and is still open there STRETCHES to span the gap; one that ends exactly at the point stays put (stretch it yourself if you want it covering the new bars). One ⟲ undoes the whole thing.
Space
Play / stop, Logic-style — anywhere except while typing in a text field. With a hardware keyboard on iPad too.
Hardware keyboard
Logic's keys: Return back to the start (or the cycle's start), K click on/off, C cycle on/off, R record, Q quantizes the selection, ⌘← / ⌘→ zoom out / in around the cursor. Editing: ⌘A selects every visible note, ⌘C / ⌘X / ⌘V copy, cut, paste at the playhead, ⌘D duplicates the selection right after itself (whole bars when it's longer than a beat — press again to keep repeating), ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z undo / redo, ⌘S Save Version, arrows move, ⇧ an octave, ⌥ resizes, Delete removes.
▦ Grid
Notes move and resize on a 16th grid, or on triplet steps while a T duration is active — and the duration chips stay visible in Select, where they are that move grid, so changing it never means a trip through Pencil. Touching a note picks up its grid automatically: grab a triplet note and moves go in triplet steps, grab a straight one and they go in 16ths; tap a chip afterwards to override. View ▾ → Grid… opens a sheet: tap a number of lines per bar (say 10) and the roll redraws instantly with that many lines in each bar — and pencil entry, note drags and resizes all SNAP to those lines. Pure view-and-snap aid: no note moves, no annotation changes, the time signature stays what it is. This is how a figure the duration buttons can't spell — ten even notes across a 4/4 bar, each 0.4 beats — becomes pencil-drag from line to line; with a grid armed, a pencil tap lays down one cell — in the roll, the fall view and the score alike — so 6 lines per bar pencils quarter-note triplets and 12 pencils eighth triplets without touching the duration chips (they dim while a grid rules, and a ▦N chip appears at the end of the row naming the grid — tap it for the sheet; opening another song turns the grid off). Set the anchor right in the sheet — bar and beat, and the beat takes decimals for sub-beat starts (2.5 = the "and" of 2, 2.25 = the second sixteenth) — and the lines run from there (14.2, say), so a figure beginning mid-bar gets its lines exactly where its notes go, continuing bar after bar on that phase across the whole song. Bar lines stay drawn for orientation but stop being snap targets while the grid is armed; a bar line falling between cells is expected, not a bug. Off returns to the meter's own grid (16ths, or triplet steps while a T duration is armed). Transient by design: set it, enter the passage, set it back.
📻 Listener mode
Phones open as a PLAYER: the roll, ⏮ ▶, the readouts, speed and volume — everything else hidden, including the section/chord bands and the notes strip (unreadably small on a phone anyway), because a shared song link is for listening, not editing. A Full app button in the header brings the whole DAW back on that device (and View ▾ → Listener mode folds it away again, on any device). Send someone a ?song= link and their phone just… plays it.
View ▾ menu
Beside Edit in the header (always there, even on locked songs) — one place for every hide/show: 𝄞 Score view, ◂ Tracks, 🛠 Edit toolbar, ▦ Bottom bar, 🎹 Instrument panel, 💬 Notes strip, and ▸ Section levels with −/+ steppers (shows "2 of 3"; the gutter chevron still one-tap cycles). ✓ means visible; the menu STAYS OPEN while you flip several at once, and closes on a tap anywhere else. Every item mirrors an existing button — the buttons are the fast path, the menu is the findable one. The header itself never hides, so View ▾ is always the way back; hiding the bottom bar floats the ▴ restore button bottom-left (one tap brings everything back). The old ▾ hide buttons are gone — hiding lives here now.
Speed & volume buttons
The speed slider folded into a percentage button — tap to open the slider, tap anywhere else and it folds back (the reset chip appears when off-native). Beside it, 🔊 is a master volume the same way: tap, slide (10–200%), tap away; the setting sticks per device and the button shows the number when it's not 100%.
LCD readout
Beside Play, Logic-style: live bar and beat (counted in the declared meter's beats), the tempo at the cursor from the song's own tempo map (scaled by the speed slider), and the declared meter and key. Undeclared stays honest: meter reads "4/4?", key reads "C?" (the display default), a stored tonic reads "B♭?". On your own songs the tempo segment is tappable too — it opens a Tempo change annotation ("tempo: 120" at a bar/beat; the map applies from there, so mid-song tempo changes work; Save writes the full map into the .mid). On analyzed songs the same annotation is an OBSERVATION — it records that the music changes tempo there and leaves playback untouched (the capture's timing is measured fact). Every readout is a door: tap the tempo to open the tempo annotation governing the cursor (or declare the first one), tap the meter to open the time signature, tap the key to open the key change ruling the cursor — a stored partial opens its own note with the tonic already filled.
Blue cursor
Play starts here. Tap the bar ruler to place it, or drag its handle (triangle under the ruler). Tapping a note selects it without moving the cursor, the DAW way, so Space still plays from where you were; + Note anchors at the note you tapped. (Settings → Other brings back tap-to-move.)

NO SOUND ON iPAD?

Silent Mode
iOS mutes Web Audio (this app's sound engine) when Silent Mode is on — while YouTube keeps playing, which makes it look like an app bug. Control Center → tap the bell. Also try volume-up while playing: the ringer channel has its own volume.
Track chips (top)
Tap a chip to select its track. M mutes — the track goes silent and its notes dim, but they stay on screen and editable. S solos (only soloed tracks play). H hides the track's notes (and their score staff) without silencing them — the way to lasso or read around one part. One tap each, any time, even mid-playback, and the song remembers them (saved with its annotations, like voice and volume). Tap the selected chip AGAIN for the voice & color menu, organized by family: NES / waves (pulses, triangle, sine, saw; auto = the classic assignment, and its menu row SAYS what it resolves to for this track — "auto: pulse 50%", or "auto: chip" when the game's own sound is available), then real sampled instruments — Keys & mallets (piano, electric piano, harpsichord, celesta, music box, vibraphone, marimba, glockenspiel), Guitar & bass, Strings (solo violin/viola/cello/contrabass, the full section, pizzicato, harp), Winds (flute, piccolo, clarinet, oboe, saxes), Brass (trumpet, trombone, french horn, tuba, section), Organ & choir — 36 FluidR3 soundfont instruments, each fetched only when a track uses it and cached after, and loudness-matched to the chip voices automatically — a violin at the same velocity as a pulse now sits at the same level, so velocity stays a musical choice instead of a mixing workaround. Last in the list, Game instruments › borrows a voice from any published PS1/N64 game's library (File → 🎛 Instruments…, same source): a shortcut to Instruments in this song leads first when the open song is itself a game song with one, then every other game — tap in for All instruments (A–Z) or one of its songs (labelled by the track it plays on, when that's the song you have open), tap an instrument to hear it and assign it in one go. The menu row shows it as "GoldenEye 007 · Soft pad"; playback renders the note through the game's own sample, caching repeats, and never goes silent — a library or sample that can't be reached falls back to the track's own synth voice. Tap a family to open it, ‹ to go back; the menu opens in the current voice's family — and its color — the wide bar at the bottom shows the track's current color and opens a full color picker (any color at all), and a vol fader above it sets the track's own volume (0–150%), live while you drag — the mixer answer when one instrument dominates. On your own songs the menu also RENAMES the track (type a name, tap Rename): voice, color, and volume settings migrate with it, and Save bakes the name into the .mid. Name a track "drums" (or "kit"/"percussion") and it becomes a drum track. Both save as a normal synced annotation ("track: pulse1 voice=piano") — playback and display only, the MIDI is never touched. Many tracks wrap onto more rows; a ▾ appears beside the last chip when they overflow — first row always shows, ▾ reveals the rest, ▴ tucks them away (the transport stays pinned to the top row). The ◂ at the far left slides the whole chip cluster away when the row feels busy; ▸ brings it back (remembered). ▶ Play and ⏮ sit on this row; the 𝄞/▦ view toggle lives bottom-left in the footer. Pan: a left–right fader under the volume in the same menu; let go and it is saved as pan= on the track's annotation. An imported song's tracks arrive where the game put them (the .mid carries each channel's pan), and its chip audio is rendered in stereo from the same values.
S
Solo: hide everyone else instead.
Tap a note
Inspector shows pitch, bar & beat (counted 1e&a), length, velocity, track — and plays it, in Roll, Score and Tracks alike. That includes chip songs: during playback the NSF render IS the track's sound, so per-note synthesis is suppressed to avoid doubling, but a tap has nothing to double and sounds a synth voice. Hearing one note at a time is the point of analysis mode. On a chip song (PlayStation, N64) the tap sounds the game's own instrument for that track; other consoles and drum tracks use the synth voice.
Status line (footer)
Tap the gold status line at the bottom to read it in full, even a long one: it wraps to two lines before it has to clip at all, and tapping opens the whole message in a sheet — nothing it says is ever lost past an ellipsis. A message that also offers a copy (a chord name, a note's detail) keeps its own tap-to-copy instead, unchanged.
Copy the pitch list
When the lasso strip lists selected pitches, tap the text (or the ⧉ copy chip) to copy them comma-separated — after "Chord?", the chord name comes along too.
⊞ Lasso
Toggle on, then drag a box over notes (works in all views). Boxes ADD to the selection — draw as many as you need. Tap any note to toggle it in or out (surgical removal of a pedal or neighbor); tap empty space to clear. Shows all the pitch names, low to high — and the 8va button beside Chord? toggles the octave numbers: off collapses duplicates to bare pitch classes (C · E · G), the chord-reading view; the setting sticks. Drag the box up into the ruler to take the annotations there too, lane by lane — up to the chord row takes the chords, higher takes the section row as well, all the way up takes the text-note flags: the box draws over the ruler, the bands it covers get a gold outline (text-note flags a gold ring) for as long as the selection lives, and those ride along with ⧉ and ✂ and land with 📋; 🗑 (or Backspace) deletes them with the notes, one ⟲ restores all of it.
◯5 Circle of fifths
The classic chart, live: majors outside with their signatures, relative minors inside, diminished chords at the center, and the movable degree window (IV·I·V over ii·vi·iii over vii°). Two independent motions: drag the wheel (or ⟲ ⟳) to spin it — put any key at 12 o'clock; tap a wedge to move the degree window there. Opens with the song's key on top and highlighted. Below the wheel: the window key's signature accidentals, full scale, all seven triads, and its IV/V neighbors.
find: (pitch finder)
Pick a pitch class in the footer dropdown and every occurrence lights up across all visible channels — everything else dims, so nothing lit means a confident zero. Works by pitch class (find B♭ catches A#), shows the count and channels in the strip, and labels the degree when a key is set. Made for mode-hunting: chasing the one accidental that separates two candidate modes.
Chord?
After a lasso: reveals what chord those notes make. Hidden by default so you can name it first.
Challenge?
Tap one of your chord bands in the ruler, then tap Challenge? — opens the evidence dialog: each label tone with its role and whether it sounds (and where), extra pitches present, the per-channel note lists, and what the namer would call the whole stack. Only when you ask; extra tones are evidence, not verdicts (a pedal point shows as "extra" — correctly).
💬
Show/hide the text-note strip (the fixed slot that shows your notes as the playhead crosses them). Off frees the vertical space; setting sticks.
🎹 Instrument panel
Opens a piano / guitar fretboard strip above the footer. Lasso'd and sounding notes both light in their track's color (earliest track wins a shared pitch); a lasso'd note gets a white ring for exactly as long as it sounds — so your selection visibly fires as the playhead crosses it. Tap any key or fret to hear it and see its name — plus its scale degree once a key is declared (the readout fades after a few seconds). Guitar is standard tuning, 24 frets: your lasso'd octave lights solid gold, and every OTHER octave of the same note gets a hollow gold ring — select one F♯ and every F♯ on the neck shows — and SOUNDING notes get the same treatment during playback, so hitting ▶ lights the whole neck's worth of what's playing, not just the sounding octave. A pitch that doesn't fit the neck shows octave-folded with a dashed ring and a tiny ▴/▾ pointing at its true octave.
▼ Fall
Parked for now (2026-09-27): opening it stopped playback on the iPad, so the button is hidden until the drawing is made cheap enough; the code is all still here. When it returns — Synthesia-style view: the whole timeline turns into a vertical drop and the notes fall down into the piano keys, landing the moment they sound. Bar numbers and chord symbols ride along their lines. Lasso works here too — box the falling notes and they light up on the keys. Piano-only; tap ▼ Fall again (or the Guitar tab) to return to the roll/score.

ANNOTATIONS

Attached notes on ANY annotation
Every typed annotation — key, meter, tempo, section, chord, loop — can carry a text note: in its editor, whatever you write in the note box below the value rides along (sections have a dedicated label field, so the note box is purely the note — and key, meter, tempo, loop, and chop all show the note box too). The ✱ marker in bands and ☰ Notes says one is there. This is where the DOUBT lives — "whole-tone material, no conventional key" can sit on a key: B♭? and make the open question findable later.
+ Note
Write a note anchored at the cursor's beat — or tap 🎤 Speak and dictate it. Fill "to bar/beat" to span a range. The ⊙ highlight toggle in the note strip shades the current note's span in the timeline.
Ruler drag
Drag along the bar ruler to select a range — + Note pre-fills it, and ▶ Play cycles over it, Logic-style: playback starts from the cycle's top every time and loops just that span (any loop: annotation is ignored while it's armed). Bar lines are magnetic: land within a finger's width of a bar line and the edge snaps TO the bar (measured in screen pixels, so it works at every zoom); away from bar lines, edges snap to 16ths — zoom in when you want fine edges. Tapping or dragging the ruler never clears your note selection — select notes, set the range, audition, all without re-lassoing. Only a DRAG arms the cycle — tapping a section or chord band still selects its range for + Note, without changing playback. Grab either edge of the highlight and drag to stretch or shrink it in either direction (bar-magnetic, stays armed). When sections nest, a ▸ chevron at the ruler's left edge cycles how many levels show — fold away a drum-keying sub-label and look at just your form; folded levels still drive the Drummer (device-side view only, per song). Tapping the ruler parks the highlight (it dims but survives); tap inside the dimmed span to re-arm it without redrawing, or drag a new span to replace it. While a cycle is armed, ⏮ returns to the cycle's start instead of bar 1. The playhead's triangle handle under the ruler is draggable in any mode. On any song, drag a section or chord band by its edge (in its ruler lane) to move that boundary — snaps to 16ths, saves like any other edit, and ⟲ undoes it. Bands are your annotations, not the music, so this works on captures and FF1 songs too; the .mid is never touched.
Gold flags
Existing annotations. Tap one to jump there and read it in the strip above the footer. They also appear as subtitles during playback.
☰ Notes
Every annotation in the song, grouped by type — key, meter, sections, chords, loop, text notes. Tap a row to edit or delete it; each group's + adds one of that type. Shortcut: double-tap a section or chord band in the ruler to open that annotation directly. Changes to synced notes need a Sync to become permanent.
Loop points
Some songs loop back past an intro (not to bar 1). When you discover one, write a note whose text is loop: B.Q (e.g. "loop: 2.1") — the note's anchor is the jump point: when playback reaches it, it returns to B.Q. If the anchor sits at/before the target, the jump happens at the song end instead.
Sections
Colored bands in the ruler (A, B…). Make one: select a range, + Note, tick "section", give it a short label. Nest them by containment. Tap a band to select its whole range. Sections and chords each get their OWN row group (sections above, chords below), so a section and a chord covering the same bars never fight for a lane.
Chords
Chord bands — like sections, but typed. Select a range, + Note, "Chord", then tap chips (root · ♭♮♯ · quality · extensions · /bass) or type the symbol. Bare root = major, m = minor (Gm). The quality row picks ONE (maj/m/dim/aug/sus2/sus4/5); the extensions row STACKS — tap 7 and add9 on top of m for Cm7add9, tap again to remove one. Anything the chips can't spell, type into the box — the label is free text and typing always wins. Same label = same color, so a recurring chord is spottable at a glance. Add an optional text note to a chord — it shows as ✱ on the band. On YOUR songs, moving a selection of EVERY note in the song takes the entire annotation layer with it — sections, chords, the loop point and its target — with chord and key labels transposing on vertical moves (global facts like meter and tempo keep their bar-1 anchor); that's how you cut an intro and slide everything left without orphaning your analysis. Moving a selection that carries one band's every note takes that band along (position slides, label transposes — Cm dragged up two semitones becomes Dm), When YOU ask for it — the Check labels button in ☰ Notes' CHORDS group — the app compares each label against what sounds in its span and flags mismatches (⚠ on the band, the reading in the list). It never volunteers this and never rewrites your labels; any note edit clears the flags. The check hears EVERY pitch sounding in the span, so passing tones and dense textures can read as "no standard chord match" — a flag is a nudge to listen, not a verdict.
No accidental duplicates
Re-labelling replaces, it doesn't stack. A key at a beat that already has one replaces it — but a key at 3.1 and a key at 3.3 are two different keys and both stand, so a mid-bar modulation keeps its real anchor. A chord band on the exact same span replaces whatever was there, whatever its label; a shorter band starting at the same beat is left alone. Text notes stack freely — several different thoughts at one anchor is the normal case — and only a repeat of the identical text at the identical anchor is dropped. Sections are untouched by this: nesting is by containment.
Chop
Trim a song without touching the file: put the cursor at the cut, + Note, "Chop", pick "everything before this beat" or "this beat to the end". The chopped part vanishes entirely and bars renumber (chop a 2-bar intro and old bar 3 becomes bar 1 — your annotations shift with it). Delete the chop in ☰ Notes to restore. Made for cleaning up freshly imported captures.

KEYS

key: picker
Songs display in C until YOU set the key. First dropdown is the tonic pitch only; black keys offer three options — fused "A♯/B♭" (spelling undecided) or either asserted spelling. Second dropdown is the mode (major, minor, and the church modes). With both set, the signature previews live — the right key makes most accidentals vanish — and the button writes it ("Set Gm @ bar 1"). Set a different key mid-song for key changes; the score draws the new signature there.
mode? (partial keys)
Know the tonic but not the mode yet? Choose "mode?" and Store writes "key: B♭?" — recorded, listed under KEY in ☰ Notes, but NOT applied: no signature, no respelling, until you return with the mode. The dropdown label always says which state the song is in.
Check vs file
In ☰ Notes, the KEY and METER groups each carry a Check vs file button — on every song, capture or composition alike, tapping it never reveals anything by itself. It compares what YOU declared against the label some MIDI files carry on their own (a game rip's own meta, an export from another program) and reports one of: your answer matches, the file's label says something else, it matches for only part of the song, you haven't set an answer yet to compare, or this file carries no label of its own — file labels can be wrong (many programs default to C major / 4/4), so a difference is a nudge to listen again, not a correction. In Normal mode it also states the file's own value plainly and — for key — the note-census estimate, plus a one-tap Use the file's button (key: adopts it as a declared key: immediately; meter: opens the meter editor pre-filled with it, same re-bar confirmation as any other meter change). Learning mode never shows the file's value or runs the estimate here — the check only ever says whether your own answer matches, never what the answer is.
Edit row
On your own songs (never on captures) a dedicated row appears above the footer: Select / Pencil / Erase (tap the active tool again to turn it OFF — then dragging only pans, and no note can be grabbed by accident), durations 32nd–whole incl. dotted, plus 16· (dotted 16th) and 8T/16T triplets — picking a triplet also switches the snap grid to triplet steps, and the grid only goes 32nd-fine when the song actually CONTAINS 32nds — to add the first one, pencil it on the beat (the grid upgrades the moment it exists) and drag it where it belongs (Logic's grid-division trick: your 4/4 stays 4/4, entry just lands on thirds until you pick a straight duration again), p/mf/f velocity, the ♮♯♭ accidental segment in score view, and ⟲ undo.
● Record
On your own songs: tap the chip of the track you want to record onto, then ● beside Play arms the take — the 🎹 panel opens, ● blinks red, the transport rolls (count-in applies), and every key you play lands on that track at the playhead — hold a key for a long note, slide across keys for runs — or play a REAL MIDI device (a Jamstik, a keyboard): the browser's MIDI input records with your actual velocities, chords included (Chrome/Edge on the computer; Safari in a browser has no Web MIDI). A MIDI keyboard works on the iPad app too — its WKWebView has no Web MIDI either, so the app ships its own native MIDI bridge instead (CoreMIDI under the hood); plug the keyboard in and it shows up here exactly like a computer's would, no browser needed. Recording keeps what you played (Logic/GarageBand/Cubasis convention): starts and durations land exactly where you played them, on- or off-grid, not snapped — Settings → Other → Snap while recording (default off) restores the old always-on-the-grid input for anyone who wants it. Either way, straighten a take afterward with Q Quantize (below) instead of fighting the grid while playing. ● again or ■ stops; the whole take is one ⟲ step. ● also says what it sees in the status line: your MIDI inputs by name; no MIDI inputs found when nothing is plugged in or the browser can't see it (Chrome lists what it sees at chrome://settings/content/midiDevices); MIDI blocked when the permission prompt was dismissed — allow it from the icon in the address bar and reload; or no Web MIDI on Safari.
Pencil drag
In Pencil mode, tap places one grid-unit of note — or keep dragging and the note stretches under your finger, snapped to the duration grid. The duration picker is note value × modifier: pick 1/2/4/8/16/32 (whole through 32nd), then — (plain), · (dotted), or T (triplet) — every duration a staff can write, two taps. A tap lands the note in the CELL you touch: press anywhere in a gap and the note starts at that gap's gridline, no edge-hunting.
Drum chart (score view)
The kit renders as a real percussion staff at the BOTTOM of the score: percussion clef, positions are roles not pitches (kick in the bottom space, snare in the third, toms by size, hats above the top line), x-noteheads for hats and cymbals, stems up for hands and down for feet. Read-only for now — kit entry lives in the roll's drum lane; lasso and tap work on the chart like anywhere else.
Score entry
Pencil and Erase work on the engraved score too: tap a staff position and the note lands there — the stave you tap picks the track, the height picks the pitch (ledger lines included), and the key signature supplies sharps/flats automatically. The key/♮/♯/♭ segment overrides the signature when you want an accidental. Erase taps a notehead out.
Move
Select notes (lasso or tap one), then drag them — up/down transposes, left/right slides in time on a 16th-note grid (triplet steps while a T duration is active), and the whole selection moves together, so a chord moves as a chord. Works straight from lasso mode: start the drag on a selected note. Keyboard: arrows (Shift+↑↓ = octave).
Resize
Drag a selected note's right edge to change its length, or its left edge to move the start while the end stays put — every selected note adjusts by the same amount, so "play this chord half as long" is one gesture. Notes too small on screen to have edge zones are all move-handle — zoom in to resize them. Keyboard: Option+←→.
Copy
A real copy and a real paste: ⧉ copies whatever is lasso'd (or tapped) — and when the lasso box itself reaches up into the ruler over them, the chord bands, section bands and text notes it spans ride along, so a copied phrase pastes with its labels (a box that stays among the notes, or a tapped selection, copies notes only; chord labels transpose if Paste to… shifts the pitch; key, meter, tempo and track directives never copy) — ✂ cuts (copies to the clipboard AND deletes — lasso'd annotations included — one ⟲ restores all of it), 📋 pastes at the blue cursor and moves the cursor to the end of what landed, so the next 📋 (or ⌘V) chains straight on; Edit ▾ → Paste to… is the richer paste: the same clipboard, onto a track you pick, shifted by octaves and/or semitones — the bass line's exact rhythm onto pulse2 an octave up, or up a third for a harmony, in one go instead of paste, move, retrack — and the copy SURVIVES scrolling, changing selection, even changing tools, so "lasso bar 3, scroll to bar 16, paste" is exactly three gestures. ⌘C fills the same clipboard. Pasting and chord inserts never stack an identical note on an existing one. For stacks from older drafts, 🧹 Remove duplicate notes in the ⇄ sheet sweeps the whole song (within each track; deliberate unisons BETWEEN tracks are always safe) — then SAVE, so a stale draft can't resurrect them. A chord progression is pencil one chord → ⧉ → 📋 at each cursor stop. Buttons that can't do anything right now are grayed — no selection grays copy/delete/split/join/⇄, an empty clipboard grays paste, empty histories gray ⟲⟳. With a keyboard there's also Option-drag (drags out an in-place copy) and ⌘C/⌘V.
Insert chord (♫)
Tap ♫ in the edit row: pick a root, a quality (maj, m, 7, maj7, m7, dim, sus… — triads insert three notes, sevenths four), an octave, and a duration (16th to whole, dotted included), then Insert — the whole chord lands at the blue cursor on the selected track, a matching chord band appears in the ruler, and the cursor walks forward one slot. Repeated inserts build a progression without closing the dialog; the inserted notes arrive selected, ready to nudge. The dialog's Progression tab holds a library of whole progressions organized by emotion — triumphant, yearning, ominous, grieving, and twenty more, in Roman numerals so they work anywhere: the tonic pre-fills from the song's declared key when there is one; pick octave and duration, tap a mood, and the entire progression lands one chord per slot with matching chord bands in the ruler, all selected, one ⟲ step. Stretch or rearrange afterwards. Or type your own in the box above the list — i – VI – VII – V, hyphens or commas or spaces all fine, lowercase for minor chords, ♭/♯ (or b/#) in front, °/7/maj7/6 after — and pick the scale the numerals count against: minor scale makes VI and VII the natural-minor degrees (in E: C and D), major scale reads them the textbook way (C♯ and D♯, so write ♭VI there). A minor key at the cursor pre-selects minor. Full chords land; erase tones to leave the arpeggio you want. The same mood list is also behind the Progressions button in the ◯5 dialog, for browsing while analyzing.
Transpose
Lasso notes → ⇅ (behind ⋯, or Edit ▾): half/whole-step chromatic buttons, octave jumps (▲/▼ 8va), plus in key ▲/▼: every note moves one SCALE DEGREE of the declared key — the "whole step up that stays in the key," where some notes move 1 and some move 2. Out-of-scale notes slide chromatically; no declared key = chromatic with a warning. For a WHOLE track, open its voice & color menu (tap the selected chip again) — the octave ▼/▲ 8va row shifts every note on that track, one tap per octave, each tap one ⟲ step. "What if the bass lived three octaves up?" is three taps, no lassoing, no muting. Notes at the range edge stay put; the drum track never transposes (kit pitches are instruments, not notes).
Move to track (⇄)
Select notes and tap ⇄, then pick a track — the notes switch instrument, keeping their time and pitch (play a passage into one voice, then deal melody, harmony, and bass out to pulse1/pulse2/triangle). When the selection spans several tracks (doubled unisons), a move only row lets you move just one track's copies and leave the others — or solo a track BEFORE lassoing: hidden tracks can't be selected at all.
Drum fill (🥁)
Tap 🥁: a one-bar step grid for kick, snare, and hat, sized to your meter (8ths or 16ths), pre-seeded with a standard backbeat. Toggle cells, set the range — bar typed, beat and 16th-subdivision (· e & a) picked from dropdowns, pre-filled from the cursor, so drums can enter at bar 2 beat 4 exactly — and Fill: the pattern repeats from that point on the drums track (created automatically if the song has none), skipping hits that already exist. One ⟲ undoes the whole fill; embellish afterwards with the pencil in the kit lane.
Split
Select notes and tap 🔪. If the blue cursor sits inside them (tap the ruler to place it), each selected note the cursor crosses splits at that exact spot; if the cursor is elsewhere, each selected note splits in half.
Join
Select two or more notes on the same pitch and tap ⁀ — they merge into one note spanning first start to last end (each pitch merges separately, so a lassoed pair of chords joins into one longer chord).
Unsaved dot
A gold ● after the title means the song has edits that haven't been published — it appears the moment you change anything and clears when Publish sheet succeeds (the Save sheet's title says which state you're in, too).
🎲 Drummer
The 🎲 beside 🥁 in the edit row (also Edit ▾ → Drummer…) generates a kit part for a bar range (prefilled from the ruler selection if one is armed, else the section under the cursor). It reads the structure YOU declared: a fixed backbeat skeleton (kick on 1, meter-aware snares) that seeds never move, hats whose loudness always stays under the snare, kicks that follow the bass track's offbeats, accents on chord-change downbeats, a snare on the bass's LONG notes (the agogic accent), fills from a small vocabulary before section boundaries and the loop target (crash on the arrival), and SILENCE in breaks — a bar where only the bass plays, or a section labeled "break", gets no drums at all. Each take REPLACES the range's kit notes and is exactly one ⟲ step, so your hand-placed drums come back with one undo. 🎲 again rerolls; the take chips replay any earlier take exactly (seed, energy, and range all remembered). Five knobs, Logic's split: busy (1–5) is density — hat subdivisions, ghosts, how eagerly kicks chase the bass; hard (1–5) is loudness — one uniform velocity shift across the whole kit, hats never dropping back below audible; fills (off–5) alone decides how often fills fire and how big (1–2 the quiet vocabulary, 4–5 runs/tom-drops/the full-bar buildup); follow picks what the kick listens to — any track, by name (its offbeat onsets and long notes, probabilistic; defaults to the detected bass) · chords (a kick exactly on every DECLARED chord change, deterministic, capped 4/bar) · off (skeleton and fills only); feel sets the backbeat rate — half (one big snare mid-bar, thinner hats: the slow-heavy read) · double (kick every beat, snare every offbeat 8th: the skank/D-beat read — bass-follow stands down, every slot is owned). The parts chips scope a reroll — kick, snare, hats, and fills (a role, not a pitch: the whole fill-and-crash layer at your section boundaries, snare runs and tom drops included). Toggle any combination: all four = the normal full roll; "I love these snares, reroll just the kick" = tap snare and hats and fills off; fills alone rerolls just the boundary bars (with fills set to off, that STRIPS the fills and lays plain groove — a de-fill). With the fills chip off the fills knob dims (nothing to control) and kept pieces stay byte-identical, hats capping under your real snares. Take chips now show their recipe (busy/hard/fills, ½ or 2× for feel, part initials when scoped) and still replay exactly. Layout: busy and hard are 1–5 segment rows (how much / how loud), fills off–5 and feel sit below, follow and parts under those — the long explanation you used to scroll past lives here in Help now. Two more rules: sections sharing an EXACT label share their groove — label two spans "A1" and the drums restate bar-for-bar (fills and crashes still vary: a fill is commentary on what comes next), so the same-label-same-color convention now also means same-drums; and at fills 4–5 the vocabulary opens its metal tier — a 16th-rate tom run down the kit, a full-bar crash-in kit fall, and a double-kick burst — weighted so big fills dominate the top of the knob.
✦ Fill
Stuck on a few bars? The ✦ beside 🎸 (behind ⋯, or Edit ▾ → Fill with AI…) opens the Ask sheet with a fill onto row: the range is the ruler selection if one is armed, else the bars in view, and the target defaults to a NEW track unless an existing track is empty there — it never silently overwrites your notes; the status line says exactly what a take replaces (by onset; a note sustaining in from before the range survives). Type what you want ("chords under the melody", "a walking line into the V", or nothing — it will fit something), then tap ✦ Fill instead of Send. The model answers in the ruler's own bars and beats, the app checks every note (inside the range, a real pitch, in a playable register) and sends bad takes back for a fix up to three times, then the notes land IMMEDIATELY on the target track as one ⟲ step — exactly the Drummer's and Bassist's contract: play it, and one undo brings back what was there. Take chips (up to 8, this session) re-apply any earlier try; Fill again for another. If your ask leaves it unsure — stacked chords or one note at a time? — it asks instead of guessing; answer with Send, then Fill again. Its one-line reasoning stays behind a why? tap (naming what it did is your job first). Only on your own songs; never drums (that's the Drummer's); nothing it writes becomes an annotation.
Edit menu
An Edit ▾ menu appears beside File on songs you can edit: ⟲ Undo, ⟳ Redo, ⧉ Copy, ✂ Cut, 📋 Paste at cursor, 📋 Paste to… (another track, another octave), 🗑 Delete, 🔪 Split, ⇅ Transpose (chromatic, octave, and in-key moves live in its sheet), ♫ Insert chord, ⇄ Move to track, 🥁 Drum pattern, 🎲 Drummer, ➗ Divide, ⁀ Join, Q Quantize — the same actions as the edit-row icons, labeled. The row itself keeps the heavy-use tools up front and folds the rest behind ⋯ (tap to expand; the choice sticks per device) — so pencil mode's duration picker fits on one iPad row again. Redo replays what Undo took back; making any new edit clears the Redo history (standard editor behavior).
Velocity
The vol slider in the edit row (1–127, the number beside it shows the value) sets the pencil's loudness — and with notes selected in Select mode, dragging it adjusts ALL of them live, brightness tracking the drag, committing one ⟲ step when you let go. Tap a selection (or a single note) and the slider jumps to its current velocity — and when every selected note shares one velocity, the selection readout says so ("… 6 notes · vel 80").
Delete
Tap 🗑 in the edit row — every selected note goes at once. Delete key does the same.
Divide (➗)
Select notes, tap ➗, pick N (2–7): each note becomes N equal notes — pitch, velocity, and total span unchanged. This is how triplets happen: 3 on a half note = quarter-note triplets (the 1 · 1.667 · 2.333 placement no grid offers), 3 on a quarter = eighth triplets, 6 on a held two-beat note = a run of six. The pieces are free notes — drag them anywhere after.
Quantize (Q)
Select notes, tap Q Quantize (behind ⋯, Edit ▾, or the Q key) and pick a strength — 100% snaps each note's start exactly onto the current grid (the same grid Move/Pencil use: 16ths, triplet steps with a T duration active, or 32nds once the song has any); 75%/50% moves it only partway there, a soft nudge for a take that's close but not glued down. Also quantize note ends additionally snaps each note's END and resizes to match — off by default, so a raw take's durations stay as played and only the onsets straighten. This is Logic's Quantize command: it acts on a selection AFTER the fact, undoably (one ⟲ step for the whole batch) — recording itself keeps what you played (see ● Record); Quantize is how you straighten it out when you want to.
Undo
Every gesture above — move, resize, copy, paste, delete, divide — is exactly one ⟲ step, and so is every track change: voice, color, volume, pan, M / S / H. Keyboard: ⌘Z undoes, ⇧⌘Z (or ⌘Y) redoes, when you're not typing in a box. Everything that adds or removes notes is one step — pencil, erase, paste, split, join, chord and progression inserts (bands included), a recorded take, Drummer and Bassist takes — and so is adding or deleting a track: ✕ Delete track is one ⟲ away, and a kit or bass track a generator created leaves with its take.
Install on the iPad
Safari → Share → Add to Home Screen. Night Roll then launches from its own icon, full screen with no browser bars, works offline (the app and any song you have opened are kept on the device; instrument sounds are kept as they are first used), and its drafts, annotations and settings live in storage Safari does not evict. Updates arrive on the next launch with a network — the page is always fetched fresh when it can be. Same for Chrome/Edge on a computer (the install icon in the address bar). File → the "build" line at the bottom of the menu says "installed" when you are running the installed copy. If offline support ever misbehaves, open the site with ?sw=0 once to turn it off on that device.
File
Everything file-shaped lives here now. File → Settings has four tabs — Saving (folder or Files), AI, GitHub, Other (the debug log) — and reopens on the one you last used. Open… (the song picker, two sections: LOCAL, this device's copies grouped by folder, each row saying not published / published / changed since publish / annotations changed here; and PUBLISHED, the albums in your repo as folders, e.g. Imports › Mega Man 2 — a published song with a local copy opens the local one; the current song's title shows above the track chips, led by Published or Local — the same meaning as Open's two sections — then its folder: Published › Final Fantasy I › Battle Scene), New song (tempo/meter → a blank 3-voice composition called Untitled N; it lives on this device until Save Version asks for a folder and a name — pick one of your folders or type a new one, NES/My Covers nests), Save Version (⌘S: a dated snapshot of the music AND annotations, kept on this device only — File → Versions… lists them), Publish (opens the Publish sheet: on your own songs its button commits the .mid AND the annotations together in one go; on analyzed songs the same door publishes the annotations — one workflow, and what gets pushed is whatever the mode owns), Save As (a copy of ANY song, including a locked capture, into the folder you pick, annotations inherited — write a counter-line over Town), Settings… (the AI model; GitHub as a two-step setup — your songs repo and a fine-grained token, with Check confirming the pair can publish; the local folder; and under advanced an optional NSF repo for imported game files — every field saves itself when you leave it; there is no Save button), Versions… (the published copy at the top when there is one, then this device's dated versions newest first — Go back to this on any row: your current state is kept as a version first, so nothing is thrown away, then that version becomes what you see — for when local edits went somewhere you can't undo your way out of), Rename… (works on everything: an uncommitted draft renames its actual file; a committed/repo song keeps its filename — analysis docs and the capture pipeline reference it — and gets a display-title override written to its album.json and the manifest, so the new name shows everywhere), Import… opens the import hub (below) — one screen, one section per format Night Roll reads, each saying exactly what it needs with its own Choose files… (one shared picker underneath — a file lands in whichever section's byte-sniff it matches); a drop target in the hub takes dragged files too, Download .mid (exports any song, works in Logic), Download audio (bounces the song to a 16-bit WAV offline — faster than real time, silent to you, no need to keep quiet hands: the song once through, loop off regardless of an armed cycle, through the same voices/chip/sampled/game-instrument/recording paths playback uses. On the iPad app it hands the file straight to the share sheet — Files, Messages, AirDrop, anywhere; in a browser it downloads. A browser with no offline renderer falls back to today's real-time capture instead — m4a on Safari / webm on Chrome, still loop off, still shareable anywhere including iMessage — and says why it fell back). Compositions auto-draft to this device on every edit — find them under Open → LOCAL, in their folder, where a ✕ (tap twice) deletes the local copy from this device; Publish is what puts them in the repo, and it updates the dropdown's catalog automatically. Drafts is not a folder — it's this device's working copies. A song you've saved lives in its album (new songs go to Night Roll Sketches) AND keeps a drafts row here; each row says which: never saved (exists only on this device, no folder yet), not published (a local copy with no published counterpart), published (matches the published copy), changed since publish (local edits not yet published), or annotations changed here (only the notes differ). Imported MIDI files land there too (prefixed "local /") — they persist on this device and stay editable, but never sync to the repo; Save As forks one into a real composition. Move to… relocates a composition into any folder of yours, or a new one (files + catalog together on GitHub for a published song; a never-published song just changes folder on this device; the row names the song's current folder first); leaving Sketches adds a "moved from" note at bar 1, which is what keeps the song editable on your other devices (as "forked from" does for Save As), so leave it in place. A ＋ track chip appears in the track bar on compositions — and a ＋ drums chip adds a GM drum kit track: its the kit gets its own labeled LANE that starts docked under your lowest melodic note — and you can DRAG it anywhere by its labels in the left gutter; the position saves as a normal synced annotation ("lane: N"), so it follows the song to every device. The working trio — hat, snare, kick — sits at the TOP of the lane, closest to your notes; below them only pieces the song actually uses appear (no toms in the song, no tom rows), and the ⋯ row under the lane toggles the full 15-piece kit when you want to pencil something new (sticks per device). Tap a piece's gutter label to cycle normal → solo → mute (S in gold / ✕ dimmed; session-only, notes untouched): one tap on snare and ONLY the snare plays; solo more pieces to add them; use mute for "everything but the kick." Third tap returns to normal. Closed hats are bright (high-passed) so they cut through regular instruments instead of fighting the pulses for the same band. Delete any track from its voice & color menu (tap the selected chip again → ✕ Delete track, tap twice), penciled like any notes, played with the built-in kit, and exported on MIDI channel 10 so Logic reads them as drums. File → Open… re-reads the published list each time you open it (at most once every 20 s), so a song published from the terminal or another device appears without relaunching. A track-name playlist (.m3u) picked on its own, with no import running, names the open song's album after the fact: each line names the song with that chip slot number — local drafts are renamed in place, a published album gets its titles in one write. Settings → GitHub → game files & instruments is the repo your published imports' game files (and the instruments pulled from them) go to; create mine makes a public one named night-roll-archive under your account. 🎛 Instruments… lists every published PlayStation and N64 game whose instruments were extracted — Instruments in this song leads when the open song is one of them, then every game; a game opens to All instruments (A–Z) or one of its own songs (labelled by the track it plays on when that's the song you have open); tap an instrument to hear it (a kit plays its first drums). Names are measured guesses. Any track in your own song can BORROW one as its voice — the voice & color menu's Game instruments › family, same games/songs picker; a loaded SoundFont's presets are one tap over in the same menu, under Soundfonts › (font, then a bank:program preset list) — tap one to assign it and hear it.
Import…
File → Import… opens the import hub: one screen, one section per format Night Roll reads, each saying exactly what it needs with its own Choose files… (one shared picker underneath — a file lands in whichever section's byte-sniff it matches, whichever section you tapped from); a drop target in the hub takes dragged files too. MIDI (.mid, .midi, .smf, .kar, even RIFF-wrapped .rmi — multi-select capable): ask where they belong — Keep local (this-device draft, annotations never sync) or Create album — one or many MIDIs become an album folder under drafts, audition/rename/✕ like a chip capture, and ⇪ Commit publishes them to the songs repo so annotations sync everywhere (commit rewrites the .mid as notes+tempo+meter — foreign CCs/programs are not preserved). NES: the .nsf, plus its .m3u if the rip has one (track names) — an NSF that needs an expansion sound chip (VRC6, VRC7, FDS, MMC5, Namco 163, Sunsoft 5B) is refused by name ("expansion sound chip <names> not supported") — the NES pipeline captures only the 2A03, and those songs keep their lead voices on the extra chip. Game Boy: the .gbs, plus its .m3u, same rule. Super NES: every .spc of the album, picked together — tagged lengths, so the loop scan is skipped. Genesis: .vgm/.vgz — synth voices only, no console-audio render yet. PlayStation: every .minipsf plus the one .psflib, picked together — reads Sony's own SEQ/VAB driver and Square's AKAO (Final Fantasy VII/VIII/IX, Chrono Cross); both play the console's own audio. PlayStation 2: every .minipsf2/.psf2 plus the one .psf2lib, picked together — reads Sony's stock driver (SQ/HD/BD) and Square Enix's own (BGM/WD — Final Fantasy X); both play the console's own audio. A PS2 set that's only streamed audio (Ico, XIII) is refused: "this is streamed audio, not note data — Night Roll reads sequence data (notes), not pre-rendered streams". Nintendo 64: every .miniusf plus the one .usflib. For NES, Game Boy, PlayStation, PlayStation 2 and Nintendo 64: a playlist (.m3u) picked on its own, later, names an open song's album (or, mid-capture, renames an already-open session's tracks). Every chip pick opens the capture panel: the same pipeline that dumped the FF1 album runs the track — loop detected and trimmed, tempo grid-fitted, the hardware loop point recorded as a loop: annotation (the capture window auto-doubles, 75 → 150 → 300s, when no loop fits) — and lands as a LOCAL draft under an album named for the game; audition and rename each one, ⇪ Commit a track or the whole album — it keeps going if you leave the menu, and it all keeps running in the background (⏳ Jobs) if you close the panel too — File → Publish import still pushes every import capture across all folders at once. Chip audio is automatic: whenever the app can reach a song's NSF/GBS/etc. (the live import session, this device's cache, or the public archive), NES, Game Boy, PlayStation, PlayStation 2 and Nintendo 64 songs render through the console's own sound hardware; Genesis and Super NES play through synth voices for now. SoundFont: one .sf2 (a fan-made game font, a better piano, anything) — not tied to a song at all: it loads straight in, a copy stays on this device (works offline, no GitHub needed) and, with a game files & instruments repo configured, pushes to the archive too so your other devices can play it; files over 50 MB ask first (GitHub itself warns past 50 MB, refuses past 100). New song from a recording: one .wav/.mp3/.m4a/.aif/.flac becomes a brand-new song — Untitled N, 4/4 at 120 bpm with three empty note tracks waiting (Edit → Pencil to write against it; ♩ Tempo from this take reads the clip's real tempo whenever you're ready) — it lives on this device until Save.
Share a song
🔗 Share link in the Publish sheet hands the song's link to the share sheet (or copies it). A link is this player plus the song plus where the song lives: songs on this site need nothing more; a song published to another GitHub repo carries songs=owner/repo, so anyone who taps it hears that song from that repo, no setup — and you can open such links too (the breadcrumb then starts with 🔗 and the repo's name; everything is read-only there, your own songs are untouched, and nothing about the link is remembered). Publish also keeps a song list in the repo's README — every song as a player link, between two markers the app owns, the rest of the README untouched — so the repo page itself is the share page. The address bar is always a shareable link to the open song, and it is the song's path with no extension — …/night-roll/albums/compositions/nightroll/ambush. Add .mid to the end and the same link is the MIDI file (Logic opens it); take it off and it's the player again. Older ?song= links still open the player. The tab title and the link preview in Messages name the song first — "Threnody · Night Roll" — so a pasted link reads as the song, not the app.
Data locations
Night Roll is configured with WHERE its data lives (Sync → "Data locations ▾"): three rows — songs (.mid, album.json, catalog), analysis (.rollnotes + docs), and NSF (chip-audio source) — each with a read base URL (blank = this site; or any raw.githubusercontent.com/<owner>/<repo>/<branch> or local server) and an owner/repo write target. One fine-grained token, granted to every repo you write to, covers all commits; write errors name the repo they hit, and a 404 usually means the token hasn't been granted that repo. This is what lets another analyst point their own analysis repo at a shared songs corpus. Defaults: everything in this site's repo, NSFs from the public nsf-archive. In the iPad app "this site" is only the bundled starters, so reads default to the repo in Settings → GitHub (the same place Publish writes): your published songs, annotations and imports appear there once the repo is set; the starters come from the bundle either way.
📁 Folder on this computer
Saving without GitHub. In File → Settings, tap Choose folder… and pick a folder on this computer: from then on every Save writes the song, its annotations, and its notes dump into that folder (laid out exactly like the repo — albums/…/song.mid beside its .rollnotes.json), nothing goes to GitHub, and no token is needed. The song picker lists the folder's albums alongside the site's; a song that exists in both opens from the folder. Tick show only this folder's songs under the folder row and the list becomes yours alone — the folder plus this device's drafts, none of the site's albums; with an empty folder the app opens straight into New song instead of Overworld. A device setting: it stays on that machine. FF1 songs still load from the site — annotate one and the annotations save to your folder. Chrome may ask for the folder again after a restart: 📁 Reconnect folder appears at the top of the File menu (until you tap it, reads fall back to the site). Forget in Settings returns saves to GitHub; the files stay where they are. Needs Chrome or Edge on a computer — Safari has no way to write files, and the row says so there. In the iPad app a .mid or chip file tapped in Files, or sent with Share → Night Roll, opens here as a local draft. In the iPad app there is nothing to set: every Save also writes the song into Files on this iPad (Files → On My iPad → Night Roll, same layout), where you can copy, share or back it up, and Publish still sends it to GitHub. Brave ships the door switched off: enable brave://flags/#file-system-access-api and relaunch (the row tells you). Recordings that aren't yours belong here, not in a repo (see the design docs).
∿ Audio tracks (recordings)
A recording — a guitar take, a vocal, a phone memo, a DAW bounce — as a track next to your MIDI voices. Tap the ＋∿ chip in the track bar (compositions and local drafts; File → Import… also recognizes audio files) and pick wav, aiff, mp3, or m4a. The clip lands at the cursor's bar as a new track named after the file, with the usual chip: M, S, color, fader, rename, ✕ Delete track. Leading silence is trimmed on arrival, so the take's FIRST SOUND sits on that bar (the status line says how much it trimmed). It plays in time with the song, loops with it (a clip longer than the notes extends the song's end), and is in the exported audio. Slow it down and the pitch stays put: at any speed but 100% the take is re-rendered (time-stretched, the way a slow-downer app does it) in the background — the lane says "⏳ preparing 50% (pitch kept)…" for a moment, then it plays in tune with your notes; a device toggle in the recording sheet turns that off for tape-style, slower = lower, like chip audio. Fine for guitar and voice down to about 40%; grainier below. Tracks view shows the waveform; tap the clip to select it (the status line says file, length, where its bytes are, and where it starts), tap again to play from its start, and in Select mode hold and drag to slide it in time (16th snap, one ⟲ undoes; with no tool armed a drag pans, as with notes). Every other view shows a thin ∿ strip under the ruler marking where the recording plays. Pieces: a recording can be cut into pieces that move on their own. ✂ Split at cursor (the edit row's ✂, Edit ▾, or the recording sheet) cuts the selected piece where the play cursor is; trim by dragging a selected piece's left or right edge in Select (left trim keeps the sound where it is); Erase tap on a piece removes just that piece (the track stays); each piece drags separately. One ⟲ undoes any of it. Tap the selected chip for the recording sheet (‹ prev / next › step between pieces): nudge starts by a bar, a beat, or a 16th, offset by 10 ms or 100 ms (how far into the file the piece starts — the last hair of alignment), ⇤ Align first sound (re-trims leading silence to the current anchor), ♩ Tempo from this take (reads the beat spacing of the piece — its waveform's onsets, autocorrelated over 40–240 BPM — and offers the tempo it hears plus half and double, with how strong the read is; tap one and it becomes the song's tempo at bar 1, one ⟲ undoes; your notes keep their bar positions, so the grid moves to meet the take, which is the point; needs about four seconds of steady playing, and your own songs only — captures keep their measured tempo), ♩♩ Map the bars to this take (the other direction: the GRID bends to the recording — it finds the beats through the whole piece, groups them into bars by the meter, and shows what it found: how many bars, the tempo range, and where the first downbeat sits; Apply writes one tempo change per bar from the piece's bar onward so every bar line lands on a downbeat it heard, wobble and all; ◀ downbeat / downbeat ▶ shift which beat counts as bar 1 when it guessed wrong — the correction Logic's Smart Tempo asks for too; the piece must start on a bar line, and a first downbeat that isn't at the piece's start means a pickup: shift, or trim the piece to the downbeat first; one ⟲ removes the whole map), ✂ Split at cursor, 🗑 Remove piece, Replace file…, and ☐ someone else's recording: tick it for a band's track you play along with and it is never uploaded — GitHub removes such files on a rights holder's notice, and a public site is distribution. Storage: until you Save, the bytes live on this device only (the sheet says so; Safari can evict browser storage after a week away, so Save soon); Save writes them beside the song as <song>.audio/<file> — into your folder in folder mode, into the songs repo otherwise. Files over 20 MB get one question: store as 16-bit mono WAV (lossless for a mono source, half a stereo bounce) or import as-is. m4a/mp3 note: Safari and Chrome trim the encoder's lead-in differently, so millisecond alignment is honest only for WAV/AIFF. Not yet: recording from the mic, trimming or splitting a clip, looping a clip by itself, keeping pitch when slowing down, iPad/Safari playback of webm.
Debug log
File → Settings → Other → Debug log shows diagnostic lines in ⚠ Messages, marked [debug]: audio wake-ups after you leave the app, engine rebuilds, audio state changes. Off, only real problems raise the ⚠ chip. A message that repeats shows once, with ×N. Turn it on when chasing a silence, so Claude can see what the audio engine measured.
⚠ Messages
Copy all puts the whole log on the clipboard for pasting to Claude. Errors outlive the moment: anything warning-shaped (failed commits, unreachable NSFs, token-scope problems, even uncaught crashes) is kept in a log, and a ⚠ button appears in the footer only when the log is non-empty — tap it to read timestamped entries, Clear to dismiss. The bottom info strip still shows the latest message; this panel is where the ones you missed went.
Song links
The address bar always holds a link to the open song — copy it and anyone who opens it lands directly on that song (?song=…). Local drafts are excluded (they exist only on your device).
Save Version and Versions…
A published song is never edited in place: you edit this device's local copy. When a song of yours has no copy here, ✎ Edit locally sits where Edit ▾ would be — tap it and the local copy is made right away, no confirmation, with a footer note: editing your copy on this device — Publish sends it. Every edit is kept automatically, on this device, the moment you make it — there is no auto-save switch to turn on; nothing is ever lost to a crash. File → Save Version (⌘S) additionally adds a DATED snapshot of the music AND the annotations to this device's history for the song — the status line says "Version saved — only on this iPad" (or "this device" outside the app); the first Save Version of an Untitled song still asks for a folder and a name. File → Versions… lists them newest first, plus the Published copy at the top when the song has one — tap Go back to this on any row: your current state is kept as a version first (labelled "Before going back"), so nothing is ever thrown away, then that version becomes what you see. The gold ● after the title means not published yet (music, annotations, or chat) — Save Version never clears it, only Publish does. Not connected anywhere (no GitHub token or repo, no local folder)? Neither the ● nor the footer Publish button shows — your work is still kept automatically, and File → Publish… still opens and explains how to connect.
Publish
Your edits are kept on this device by themselves; Publish is the deliberate step that puts a song in the repo where other devices and other people can reach it. The Publish sheet (File → Publish… and the footer button open the same door) It lists every song with anything pending on this device, the open song first: a line when its music is edited since publish, each unsynced annotation on its own line with a ✕ that discards that never-synced note from this device, and a line when chat messages are unsaved. Every song's row has the same three buttons: tap Open to open it here, Publish to publish that song only (a job — ⏳ shows it), Revert to drop this device's changes to it after asking (your current state is kept as a version first — File → Versions… brings it back; a song never published has no Revert — there is no published copy to go back to). ⇪ Publish song ships the open song: .mid, .rollnotes.json, .notes.txt and .ask.md for your own songs; annotations + chat for analyzed ones. Publish all (N) appears when more than one song is pending and publishes everything pending on this device — music, annotations and chat, for every song listed. Needs your token once; Copy/Download the file otherwise. "Unsynced" = still only on this device. Repo ↗ opens the GitHub repository in a new tab. ⎘ Web session copies a bootstrap instruction — paste it into a fresh Claude Web chat and it clones the repo, reads WEB-SESSION.md from disk, and has everything it needs to run an analysis session (process rules, file locations, session shape, handoff format). It copies the clone command rather than a URL on purpose: a session that starts by fetching keeps fetching, one file at a time, and can't grep across your notes.
✦ AI
Talk to an AI tutor about what you're looking at — and, on your own songs, have it write notes (see ✦ Fill under Editor). Tap ✦ AI in the top bar. Every message you send carries the song, your cursor, the lasso, your own annotations, and the notes of the bars in view (or the ruler-selected range), so "what's happening in bar 9?" means YOUR bar 9 — bars and beats are the ones on your ruler, in your declared meter.
House rules
🎓 Learning mode (Settings → Other): hints and direction first — it confirms or refines a guess you've made, and tells you outright only when you insist or say you give up; general theory questions it answers directly; it never reveals a key you haven't set. Normal mode: it answers music questions directly — keys, chords, cadences, form — and says how sure it is; an estimated key is named as an estimate, not a fact. Either mode, it never annotates on its own initiative or answers a question you didn't ask.
Move a sheet
Where you leave a sheet is where it reopens on this device, size included (the first open is centered). Drag any sheet by its title line (AI, SETTINGS, the capture panel's title row…) to slide it aside — say, to keep the capture panel in view while you talk to the AI; drag the ◢ in its bottom-right corner to resize it. Both come back to the defaults the next time it opens.
Dock right (and left, and bottom)
Tap Dock beside AI, ALL NOTES, INSTRUMENTS, JOBS, or PUBLISH to open its menu: Left, Right, or Bottom pin it to that edge instead of a floating window — no backdrop, so you can keep working the roll (tap, edit, play) with it open, the song laid out in what's left. Once docked to a side, the same menu offers Full height (edge to edge, beside the header and footer too) or Beside the roll (the header rows above and the footer below stay full width — only the roll narrows). Drag the strip on the dock's inner edge to resize it — 280px up to nearly the whole window, leaving only a thin strip of the song's edge showing, so you can shove the roll out of the way for a minute and drag back (double-tap the strip to reset it to the default width). Dropping a window's title on a side that already holds one makes a tab group there — a small strip of tabs above it, one shown at a time; tap a tab to switch, and closing a tab's window just drops its chip from the strip (it's still docked — reopen it and the chip comes back). The bottom dock can hold two windows side by side — dock a second one there and a divider splits them; drag it to change the split, and drag the strip along the bottom dock's top edge to resize its height (160px up to nearly the whole window, same double-tap-to-reset). Float undocks a window again, right where it was — or just drag a docked window's title back out into the middle. Drag-to-dock: instead of the menu, grab a window's title and drag it to an edge — a highlight shows where it'll land (the outer part of a side edge for full height, the inner part for beside the roll); let go to dock there, or in the middle to float. Remembered on this device — reopening a window re-docks it if you left it docked; closing one frees its space without undocking it. On a phone-width window the Dock button is hidden and every window is always floating — there's no room to give the song.
⏳ Jobs
Captures and publishes run as background jobs: start one and close its panel — the ⏳ chip in the footer shows how many are running, tap it for the list (title, a progress bar, progress text like "12/92 · Frog's Theme 40%", and per job Open to get back to its panel, ✕ to cancel a running one or dismiss a finished one, ↻ to retry what is left). Done and cancelled jobs clear themselves a few seconds after they end, and the ⏳ chip itself hides once none are left; a failed or interrupted job stays until you ↻ or ✕ it — those are the ones to look at. A job never cancels because you closed its panel; it pauses while the app is in the background and picks up where it was. If the page dies mid-run, the next open marks the job interrupted with its last counts: ↻ re-runs the tracks not yet saved when the same files are still open, and says to Import them again otherwise (saved tracks are kept and skipped). One capture at a time; one publish per folder; one Publish all at a time.
Publish dialog
Starting a folder's publish from Open → LOCAL, or tapping Publish all in the Publish sheet, opens a dialog for that one job: an overall bar, a row per song (its title, and a state — … queued, a small bar while it runs, ✓ done, ⚠ failed with the error), the job's own note line, Cancel while it's running (stopping it between songs — what's already published stays published), and Close always. Closing it never cancels the job — reopen it from ⏳'s Open on that job any time. Capture jobs still open the familiar capture panel.
⧉ copy / links
Every bubble ends with a small ⧉: tap it to copy that message whole, ready to paste anywhere (it says ✓ copied for a moment). Web addresses in a bubble are tappable and open in Safari, in a new tab, so a link the AI gives you is one tap away.
🎤 Speak / ■ Stop listening / ■ Stop reply
Tap 🎤 Speak to dictate a question; while it listens the same button reads ■ Stop listening (your words still land in the box). The other stop, ■ Stop reply beside Clear chat, cuts a slow reply short and re-enables Send — Send stays disabled while a reply is cooking.
Slow replies
